Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Renewed Conflict in Tigray Raises Fears of a New Humanitarian Emergency 14 October 2026 Fides News Agency (Vatican) Adigrat — Nearly a month has passed since fighting resumed in Ethiopia, where an alliance of rebel groups led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) has launched a new offensive, reigniting a conflict that claimed hundreds of thousands of lives between 2020 and 2022. Almost four years after the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022 (see Fides, 3/11/2022), with the aim of ending the devastating war in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, renewed hostilities, reported in recent weeks, are escalating (see Fides, 30/9/2026). The Ethiopian federal army now controls much of eastern and central Tigray. According to local sources, government forces have also captured Zalambessa, a town of around 15,000 inhabitants on the Ethiopian side of the border with Eritrea. "As an ecclesial community, we are living under the weight of many pressures, tensions and anxieties. But, by the grace of God, we move forward. The situation does not look particularly promising. In our outposts, however, everything is under control, while sporadic gunfire has been reported in some towns." This is what a local source told Fides News Agency, requesting anonymity for security reasons. The renewed fighting is unfolding against a regional backdrop of increasingly tense relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. After decades of conflict, the two countries signed a peace agreement in 2018. During the Tigray war, Eritrea supported the Ethiopian federal government against TPLF forces. Since then, however, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated once again. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines One of the main sources of tension is Ethiopia's quest for access to the sea. Addis Ababa lost its direct access to the coast when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, after Ethiopia had enjoyed it for decades. The Ethiopian government regards regaining access to the sea as a strategic and vital national interest, while reiterating its intention to pursue this objective through dialogue and peaceful means. The geographical position of the two countries further heightens the significance of the dispute. Control of areas overlooking the Red Sea and the trade routes crossing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives the region considerable geopolitical importance. Beyond the renewed fighting, the humanitarian situation is a major cause for concern. Hundreds of thousands of people displaced from western Tigray have still been unable to return home, leaving around 44 per cent of the region's most fertile agricultural land inaccessible. In north-western, central and eastern areas where some farmers have managed to return, they have found farms and communities devastated by years of war. Adverse weather conditions have compounded the crisis. The first seasonal rains ended almost a month earlier than usual, compromising seed germination and causing crops to wither in numerous districts. The rains needed for the spring harvest, meanwhile, arrived more than five weeks late in eastern and southern areas, with some areas experiencing periods of drought lasting more than a month. The agricultural toll has been severe: more than 252,500 hectares of crops have been destroyed, while 140 districts are facing conditions described as catastrophic. More than 3.5 million livestock are also at risk of dying from hunger and disease following the disappearance of seasonal grazing lands and the depletion of groundwater reserves. The failure of the September harvest and the collapse in the livestock-to-cereal terms of trade have further exacerbated the crisis. According to the September humanitarian report issued by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission (DRMC), 3.9 million people--more than half the region's population--were in immediate need of emergency food assistance. The threat of another famine is once again looming over Tigray. As federal forces advanced towards the regional capital, coalition forces abandoned government buildings and police stations across the city. For around 24 hours, Mekelle was left in the grip of a serious power vacuum. Armed groups, reportedly made up largely of prisoners released after a nearby prison was abruptly abandoned, stormed and looted government buildings, post offices, art galleries and facilities providing assistance to the population. Particularly serious was the looting of infrastructure dedicated to the humanitarian response. Armed groups ransacked DRMC offices and warehouses belonging to the regional body responsible for coordinating relief operations and ensuring the provision of essential goods and services to the population. Ethiopia Secures Additional U.S.$8.5 Million in UN Humanitarian Funding
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Secures Additional U.S.$8.5 Million in UN Humanitarian Funding - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Secures Additional U.S.$8.5 Million in UN Humanitarian Funding 14 October 2026 The Reporter (Addis Ababa) By Beakal Teshome Ethiopia has secured an additional USD8.5 million in United Nations humanitarian funding to provide emergency assistance and protect civilians, with more than 202,700 people expected to benefit across regions facing acute humanitarian needs. Tom Fletcher, the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, announced the allocation on October 13 through the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). The funding will cover Tigray, Amhara, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz, alongside other areas in need of urgent assistance. The allocation comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia that the UN has warned could deepen humanitarian needs and threaten regional stability. Secretary-General António Guterres expressed concern earlier this week over clashes in Tigray, Afar and Amhara, as well as reports of Eritrean forces in Ethiopia, warning of the risk of further escalation. The UN has also raised concerns about new displacement, civilian protection and disruptions to aid operations. The allocation will prioritise people affected by new or secondary displacement, communities facing disruptions to essential services and areas where humanitarian response capacity remains limited. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie The funds will support water, sanitation and hygiene, shelter, healthcare, nutrition and protection services, as well as shared services needed to facilitate humanitarian operations. "The additional resources will complement the significant response efforts already underway by the Government and humanitarian partners," said Ozonnia Ojielo, the UN resident and humanitarian coordinator in Ethiopia. The latest allocation brings CERF's total funding for Ethiopia in 2026 to more than USD22.5 million. The funding includes support for anticipatory action in Afar and Amhara, where El Niño-induced dry conditions have created additional humanitarian concerns. Read the original article on Reporter . ethiopia.title: IMF Postpones Ethiopia Review Schedule, Board Decision Slated for Early 2027
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: IMF Postpones Ethiopia Review Schedule, Board Decision Slated for Early 2027 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: IMF Postpones Ethiopia Review Schedule, Board Decision Slated for Early 2027 14 October 2026 The Reporter (Addis Ababa) By Mintesinot Nigussie The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has scheduled discussions on Ethiopia's sixth review under its Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement for November, with a final decision from the Fund's Executive Board expected in early 2027. The schedule pushes the process beyond the previously indicated October 15 milestone. An IMF spokesperson told The Reporter that November will mark the next round of talks on Ethiopia's reform programme. However, a formal decision on the sixth review will not occur until early 2027, when the assessment is presented to the Executive Board. The spokesperson did not disclose a firm timetable for either milestone. The IMF's fifth-review report, published in July, had previously noted October 15, 2026, as the earliest date for the next disbursement--projected at SDR 154.11 million, down from the originally planned SDR 191.70 million. The spokesperson emphasized that October 15 was merely the earliest window for potential fund distribution rather than a hard deadline for concluding the review, with actual fund releases remaining strictly contingent on Executive Board approval. The review process requires an IMF mission to travel to Ethiopia to evaluate economic performance and consult with government authorities. The mission then reports its findings to fund headquarters, where the Executive Board determines whether programme conditions have been met to allow subsequent disbursements. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie In a separate exchange with The Reporter , Julie Kozack, the IMF's Director of Communications, noted that the Fund could not yet pin down a completion date, as the mission must first meet with Ethiopian authorities before presenting its assessment to the board. "What will happen before we conclude the next review is we have a mission, and a team will go to Ethiopia and talk with the authorities. They will come back and present the report to the Executive Board," Kozack said. The fifth review, completed on July 1, disbursed approximately USD 464 million and brought cumulative disbursements under the four-year, USD 3.4 billion programme to about USD 2.647 billion. The IMF reported that Ethiopia met all quantitative performance criteria for end-December 2025 and achieved most indicative targets, alongside notable progress in exports, foreign-exchange reserves, and government revenue. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia's T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia's Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) Those results, however, cover an earlier assessment period and do not dictate the outcome of the sixth review, which evaluates Ethiopia's performance against targets set for the end of June 2026. Approved in July 2024, the ECF arrangement supports Ethiopia's broader economic reform agenda, which aims to correct macroeconomic imbalances, strengthen public finances, and foster private-sector-led growth. Since entering the programme, the government has introduced income tax modifications, stepped up tax compliance and customs administration, liberalized the foreign-exchange market, and gradually reduced fuel subsidies to raise domestic revenue and relieve public finance pressures. These measures have coincided with a sharp rise in tax collection. Federal tax revenue surged by 76 percent in the first nine months of the 2025/26 fiscal year compared to the same period a year earlier, driven by adjustments to income and fuel taxes, according to IMF data. General-government tax revenue is estimated to have climbed from 6.2 percent of GDP in 2023/24 to 9.5 percent in 2025/26. During a fiscal policy press briefing on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday, The Reporter asked Davide Furceri, a division chief in the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department, whether aggressive tax hikes and subsidy cuts are appropriate for Ethiopia given its massive informal sector and structural productivity constraints. Furceri responded that nations starting from a very low tax-to-GDP base, such as Ethiopia and Nigeria, must mobilize additional domestic revenue to fund essential public spending and service debt. "For many countries that are starting from a very low tax rate base, like Ethiopia and Nigeria, it is important to raise sufficient revenue," Furceri said. Beyond expanding the tax base, Furceri stressed that governments must eliminate structural distortions in their tax systems that hamper economic activity. Addressing these inefficiencies can improve revenue collection without imposing undue burdens on the economy. He also cautioned against dismissing targeted subsidies simply because a country lacks comprehensive national registries or digital payment systems. While building such infrastructure remains a crucial medium-term priority, governments can deploy alternative strategies immediately. "Countries need to prepare for this in the medium term. In the short term, there are alternatives, including school-feeding programmes and geographically targeted support," he said. Read the original article on Reporter .
